<reason>CON built the more coherent path: the "fork" (obvious sentence / expensive right / useful-but-exploitable criteria) survived PRO's self-refutation charge, and CON's core insight—that notice only informs when it discriminates (credit adverse-action notices, boost labels, sponsored tags) while a universal always-on banner tells no one anything—was applied consistently to every PRO analogy (nutrition facts, sponsored content, credit). CON answered both pressure questions directly and substantively, naming concrete acceptable disclosures, which blunted PRO's "you reject all transparency" line and forced PRO's closing to retreat to "floor not ceiling." CON also turned PRO's attribution argument (machine-blame prompts boost purchases) and PRO never squarely answered it. PRO had real strengths—memorable "door not house" framing, the deceptive-practices complaint in A1, the daily-harm weighing, and the fair point that users don't hear "matching" as "scored for desirability"—but PRO's own B1.6 disavowed the substantive disclosure its harm story needs, and CON exploited that gap through the closing. CON's scammer argument was weak and effectively conceded, and its "everyone already knows" premise is contestable, keeping this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 turning PRO's own analogies: nutrition labels list ingredients (the criteria disclosure PRO disavowed), and sponsored labels inform because they discriminate—"a signal that's always on is not a signal." This became the spine of the debate and PRO's "apps can compete by promising not to rank" reply only partly answered it.</best_rebuttal>
